title: AI Power User: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Priya's vendor summary ran to completion and the tool reported success, but the headline total was a few hundred dollars off because the tool pulled a stale version of one vendor's numbers. Per the lesson, what is this an example of?
options: A silent error, a failure where the system does not behave as expected but surfaces no visible error, alert, or warning, so the workflow reports success while the output is wrong
A hallucination, because the tool invented a number that did not exist
A mid-flow break, because the workflow stopped partway through the run
A dry run failure, because the tool refused to produce any output
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a silent error as a situation where a system fails to behave as expected but does not surface any visible error, alert, or warning. Priya's run reported success while the total was wrong, which is exactly that. A hallucination is a fabricated claim, not a stale number; a mid-flow break is a run that stops partway; and the tool did produce output, so it is not a dry run failure.

questions.question: In the audit's three passes, what does pass three flag as a candidate for automation?
options: The tasks that have the same shape every time: the same inputs, the same steps, and the same output format
The largest or most visible task, regardless of how often it happens
The tasks that change shape each run and need your judgment
Any task a colleague mentions, starting today
questions.explanation: Pass three flags tasks with the same shape every time, the same inputs, steps, and output format. These are where a saved setup pays for itself, because every repetition after the first is cheaper.

questions.question: Priya's monthly vendor summary came back wrong: the overdue-deliveries flag was empty and the tone drifted hedged. Per the lesson, what is the most reliable way for her to work out why?
options: Consult her changelog, which records each change with a date and a reason, and trace the broken behavior back to the exact edit that caused it
Rewrite the prompt from scratch so it looks fresh and hope the regenerated output improves
Regenerate the output repeatedly until it happens to come out close to what she wants
Turn the tool off and do the summary by hand from now on without examining the cause
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that a version problem is best diagnosed by evidence: a changelog with dated, reason-based entries turns a guessing game into a lookup. In Priya's case the log showed she had moved the overdue flag into a variable slot, which is why it went missing. Rewriting, regenerating blindly, or abandoning the tool all skip the diagnosis the lesson recommends.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what are the three pieces that every custom tool worth building has?
options: Tailored instructions, saved context, and your own project
Input, tool, and output
A prompt, a template, and a calendar
Instructions, review, and archive
questions.explanation: The lesson maps the three pieces directly to the title: tailored instructions (the standing prompt), saved context (reference material the tool can consult), and your own project (the container that holds the first two together).

questions.question: According to the lesson, which combination makes a task the ideal first candidate for a workflow?
options: Frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk to get wrong
Large, impressive, and done once a quarter
Rare, complex, and high-stakes so it gets attention
Irregular, judgment-heavy, and urgent
questions.explanation: The lesson names three tests: it is frequent, it is same-shaped, and it is low-risk to get wrong. A task meeting all three is the ideal first candidate, because the setup pays off and you can trust the workflow to draft while you decide.

questions.question: A colleague asks whether she should build a reusable template for an irregular, judgment-heavy task that happens once or twice a year. Per the lesson, what is the right call?
options: Do not build it; a template only pays off when the task recurs often and the frame stays stable, and a one-off leaves the setup unused
Build it anyway because every task benefits from a fixed format
Build it and force the task to fit the frame, since templates always improve output
Build a separate template for every single variation the task could hit
questions.explanation: The lesson says a template earns its keep only when two things are true: the task recurs often enough that the setup pays for itself, and the frame is genuinely stable across runs. A rare, judgment-heavy, irregular task is exactly the case the lesson flags where a one-off prompt is the better choice. The other options recommend templates where the lesson recommends against them.

questions.question: Maya's draft step produced a LinkedIn post that opened with a confident statistic she had never seen, and when she checked, there was no source behind it. Per the lesson, what is the right diagnosis and fix?
options: It is a hallucination, a fabricated number presented as fact, so she should delete the unsourced claim or replace it with one she can verify, and log the review habit in her changelog
It is a handoff failure, so she should rewrite the data pull step to expect a different field from the calendar
It is a scheduling error, so she should change the trigger to run the workflow on a different day
It is unfixable, so she should abandon the workflow and write all content by hand again
questions.explanation: The lesson's failure story is exactly this: the draft produced a plausible, well-formatted statistic that came from nowhere, which is a hallucination, the failure mode from Lesson 11 where a model presents fabricated information as fact. The fix was not a new prompt rule but a review habit: before approving any draft that contains a number, ask where it came from, and if the draft does not name a source she can check, delete the claim or replace it with one she can verify. She logged that habit in her changelog. Rewriting the pull step, changing the trigger, or reverting to manual work all skip the diagnosis the lesson teaches.

questions.question: You are deciding whether to assemble a monthly report into a four step pipeline: trigger, draft, review gate, output. Based on the lesson, when is building this pipeline clearly the wrong call?
options: When the report is a one-off you will never run again, because the cost of the handoffs outweighs any benefit and the frame will not stay stable
When the report recurs weekly and the output shape stays the same each time
When a human should review the draft before it goes out
When the source data arrives in a consistent, predictable form every time
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the recurring-and-stable test from the choosing lesson: a job that recurs with a steady shape earns assembly, while a one-off that is never repeated does not, and forcing it into a pipeline is ceremonial weight with no payload. The recurring, gated, consistently shaped cases are the ones that justify a pipeline, not the ones that argue against it.

questions.question: A colleague who has never seen your workflow tries to run one cycle using only your runbook entry, and stops at the inputs section asking which of two similarly named folders is authoritative. What does the lesson say this outcome means?
options: The handover test worked: the stop is a missing field, and the input section needs the exact path and naming pattern written down
The colleague lacks prerequisite expertise, so the entry is complete and the failure is on their side
The runbook entry is too long and should be cut back to the ordered steps only
The workflow should be retired, because a confusing input location means the pipeline is unreliable
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the handover test as giving the entry to someone who has never run the workflow and watching where they stop, and states that every stop is a missing field. Priya's own test surfaced exactly this ambiguity about two folders with similar names.

questions.question: Maya's weekly newsletter flow broke: the draft came back slightly off because the tracker now exports client names with a bracket tag, and her template expects plain names. Per the lesson, where is the fault, and what is the right first move?
options: The fault is at the handoff between the tracker and the template, so she should name that boundary, fix the template to strip the tag, and log the change in her changelog
The fault is inside the template prompt, so she should rewrite the whole draft step from scratch without touching the trigger or the gate
The fault is in the newsletter tool, so she should change where the final output is posted before examining the steps
The fault is unfixable, so she should abandon the pipeline and do the newsletter by hand again
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that in a multi-step pipeline the fault is usually at the handoff, the boundary where one step's output becomes the next step's input. The tracker changed what it exports, and the template was consuming the old shape. Naming the boundary, fixing the consuming step, and logging the fix are exactly the moves the lesson recommends. Rewriting the whole step, blaming the output tool, or reverting to manual work all skip the diagnosis the lesson teaches.

questions.question: Dev knows the executive summary must stay one line and the section order must stay fixed. Per the lesson, what is the maintainability test that tells him the rules are coupled and need separating?
options: A change that should touch exactly one rule forces him to edit several: the same rule is stated in multiple places, or a variable inputs slot is woven into the instructions, so one edit risks silently breaking the rest
The prompt has more than one labeled section
The prompt output changes when the underlying tool gets an update
The prompt is longer than a page
questions.explanation: The lesson defines maintainability as the property that lets a single small edit change one rule without damaging the others except his change touches multiple spots, the rules are coupled: the same fact or constraint appears in scattered sentenceshare, and a variable slot is entangled with fixed instructions. That coupling is the warning sign. More sections are the cure, not the disease, and tool updates and raw length do not measure coupling.

questions.question: Which measure specifically converts a silent failure (a run that reports success while the output is wrong) into a loud one?
options: A post-run check that reconciles the flagged count in the output against the count in the source, and fails the run when they disagree
A longer retry policy so a failing step gets more attempts
A more detailed prompt so the drafting step is less likely to make mistakes
A canary period where the output goes to you before it goes to the audience
questions.explanation: The lesson names count reconciliation, field presence, and expected-content checks as the post-run checks that catch quiet failures. A canary limits blast radius and retries help recovery, but neither detects that the output itself is wrong.

questions.question: Nadia's weekly operations report came back with an impossible 99.4 percent on-time rate. She checked her changelog and found the tracker had added a new status field that the pull step was reading as blank, and the compute step was counting blank as on time. Per the lesson, what is the right diagnosis and fix?
options: The fault is at the handoff between the tracker and the pull step, so she should map the new status code to the on-time flag before the compute step reads it, then log the change
The fault is inside the compute prompt, so she should rewrite the whole compute step from scratch without touching the pull step
The fault is in the report output, so she should change where the report is posted before examining the steps
The fault is unfixable, so she should abandon the workflow and build the report by hand every week
questions.explanation: The lesson's failure story is exactly this: the tracker changed what it exports, the pull step expected the old on-time flag, and the compute step inherited the flaw. The changelog let Nadia find the change in minutes, and the fix was one line mapping the new status code to the on-time flag before the compute step reads it. This is the garbage-in, garbage-out principle made concrete: the input changed shape and the whole report inherited it. Rewriting the compute step, blaming the output, or reverting to manual work all skip the diagnosis the lesson teaches.

questions.question: Priya wants to add purchase recommendations with spend levels to her monthly vendor summary. Per the lesson, which step in her workflow should earn a review gate?
options: The data pull, because it is the foundation everything else builds on
Before a purchase recommendation becomes a suggestion, because the tool cannot see the context she holds (the pricing dispute, the pilot category) and a bad spend number is expensive to unwind
Every step in the workflow, so nothing can ever ship without a human
The formatting step, because a clean layout matters most to leadership
questions.explanation: The lesson has Priya run her workflow through the four triggers (irreversibility, low confidence, external visibility, context gaps) and gate only the steps that earn a pause. The recommendation step has low confidence as new, holds context the tool cannot see, and carries an expensive-to-unwind spend number, so it earns a gate before it becomes a suggestion. She deliberately does not gate the data pull, which is routine and reversible (it earns rhythm, not a pause), and gates, rather than leaves ungated, the customer-facing summary.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what does the input part of a workflow represent?
options: The data, information, or resources that enter the system, and the contract between the workflow and the rest of your work
The saved instruction that formats the output
The check you run before the output ships
The final result the workflow produces
questions.explanation: The lesson defines input as the data, information, or resources that enter the system, and calls it the contract between the workflow and the rest of your work: if you can name what goes in, you know what to gather before you run it.

questions.question: Priya's weekly report workflow stopped producing the finance language her team depends on after her tool vendor shipped a model update, but nothing crashed and no error was logged. Per the lesson, what does this describe, and what reveals it?
options: It is a regression, a change that makes previously working output worse, and it is revealed only by re-running her golden set of known-good cases and seeing the grade drop from 9 of 11 to 5 of 11
It is a data pull failure, so she should rewrite the source-of-truth step to expect a different field
It is a scheduling error, so she should change the workflow's trigger to run on a different day
It cannot happen because a workflow either runs or it does not, and there is no way to fail without a crash
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example is exactly this: nothing crashed, the format was unchanged, and the numbers looked clean to the review gate, but a model version change had quietly degraded the drafting step. That is the definition of a regression, a change that makes something that was working correctly stop working correctly. It was revealed only because Priya re-ran her golden set of eleven cases, and the accuracy that was 9 of 11 dropped to 5 of 11. The other options confuse the regression with a pull failure, a scheduling error, or deny that it can happen at all.

questions.question: Priya is choosing between two tools for her weekly client report. A new tool with heavy marketing promises "99.9 percent uptime" and an "SLA," but its status page shows almost no history and no post-mortems, while the model she already uses has months of documented incident history she has watched and logged. Per the lesson, why should the new tool's empty status page give her pause?
options: Because an empty incident history means she has no track record to grade, so she would be trusting a promise with no evidence behind it
Because a short status page history is proof the tool is deliberately hiding a major outage
Because any tool that has not been through an outage is fragile and guaranteed to fail soon
Because the vendor's "99.9 percent uptime" figure contradicts the empty status page, so the tool is actively lying
questions.explanation: The lesson says an empty incident history is not proof a tool is fragile, but it is proof you have no evidence either way, which means you would be trusting a promise with nothing behind it. A power user grades a tool by its track record, not by assuming the best from a missing one.

questions.question: Per the lesson, which habit is what makes a rollback possible at all?
options: Never overwriting the version that works: save a known-good baseline and always work on a copy, so any new change can be undone by returning to it
Keeping every edit in one running file so the most recent version replaces the older one every time
Recording only the changes that turned out badly and ignoring the rest
Writing every change without a date so the sequence is shorter and easier to scan
questions.explanation: The lesson says the human translation of Semantic Versioning's 'contents must not be modified' rule is: keep the good version intact and never edit it in place, save the new attempt as a new version so the known-good baseline survives to be rolled back to. Overwriting, recording only failures, and dropping dates all contradict that and make rollback impossible or misleading.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does an audit beat guessing from memory about how you spend your week?
options: Because memory flatters: you overestimate engaging or urgent tasks and underestimate quiet, repetitive ones, so an audit measures the week as it actually ran
Because an audit is faster than thinking about your work
Because memory is always wrong about everything, so any measurement is better
Because an audit tells you which tasks to stop doing entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson says your intuition is systematically wrong in one direction: you overestimate engaging or urgent tasks and underestimate quiet, repetitive ones. The audit corrects that by measuring the week as it actually ran.

questions.question: Marcus's five-whys analysis ended with the finding that his workflow had no check for empty input, so an empty data read looked like a normal run. Per the lesson, what is the root cause of the failure?
options: The missing check for empty input, because it is the underlying condition Marcus can actually fix, while the format change is only the proximate cause he cannot fully control
The data source's format change, because that is the immediate trigger that happened right before the failure
The email step, because the report never reached the client's inbox
Marcus's carelessness in building the workflow, because a better builder would have predicted the format change
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes proximate cause from root cause: the format change is the proximate cause, the immediate trigger Marcus could not have predicted and cannot fully control, while the missing check for empty input is the root cause, the underlying condition he can fix today. The five whys exist to reach the root cause, not stop at the proximate one.

questions.question: What three moves does Hamid make to turn his personal budget-variance workflow into a team one?
options: Broadcast it to the whole team at once, move the data files into a shared drive, and remove the review gate to save time
Adapt the record for a stranger, test it with one real second user before inviting the rest, and decide what data the workflow is allowed and not allowed to touch
Rewrite it in a lower-level programming language, document every edge case, and assign each teammate a different version
Share only the output template, keep the processing steps private, and let each analyst build their own flow
questions.explanation: Hamid adapts the runbook entry for a stranger, tests with one teammate (Priya) before inviting the other three, and names ownership and data rules. Small rollout with a real second user plus explicit data governance is the lesson's sharing pattern.

questions.question: A vendor advertises "99.9 uptime" for its API. When Priya reads the fine print, missing the number earns an apology rather than a refund or credit. Based on the lesson, how should she classify this promise?
options: It is an SLO, a target value that carries no explicit consequence when missed, even though it is advertised as an SLA
It is an SLA, because the vendor put a specific percentage in writing
It is an SLI, because it is a measurable number like error rate or uptime
It is an error budget, because it tells her how much downtime the vendor is allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the test: ask what happens if the number is missed. If the answer is a payout or penalty, it is an SLA; if it is just an apology, it is an SLO. A percentage in writing does not make it an SLA against the lesson's rule. An SLI is the measured indicator, and an error budget is the allowed amount of failure built into a target.

questions.question: Priya adds last year's data to her weekly report and the model silently leaves out a region. Nothing errors, the output just comes back shorter with a region missing. Per the lesson, what happened and what is the right fix?
options: The input exceeded the model's context window, so the model truncated or set aside the oldest part, and the fix is to feed a compact summary of the data instead of every row
She hit a rate limit on requests per minute, and the fix is to wait and retry later
She exceeded her monthly spend limit, and the fix is to raise the cap
The golden set from Lesson 18 flagged a regression, and the fix is to roll back the drafting step
questions.explanation: The lesson says the context window is the amount of text a model can consider at once, and when data exceeds it, the model must truncate or summarize before proceeding, which happens without announcing itself. Priya's added data pushed the input past the window, so the oldest part was set aside. She fixed it by feeding a compact summary table of last year's totals instead of the firehose. A rate limit shows an error, a spend limit shows up on the bill, and a golden-set regression gives a wrong number, not a dropped region.

questions.question: Priya finds she has written four slightly different versions of her house-style voice and tone rules, one at the start of each workflow. Per the lesson, what is the correct move?
options: Keep all four so each workflow always has its own personal copy
Merge them into one authoritative house-style instruction that every workflow references instead of carrying its own
Delete the instructions entirely so the tool writes in whatever tone it wants
Write a fifth, longer version and add it to every workflow
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the DRY principle here: keeping one authoritative copy of each piece of knowledge, referenced everywhere, is the discipline that stops libraries from rotting, because one edit fixes the style everywhere instead of four. Keeping four copies, deleting them, or adding a fifth longer one all describe duplication the lesson explicitly warns against.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what should the honest review of a workflow compare before deciding to retire it?
options: The hours it saves on a good day against a fixed budget target
Whether it usually works against whether it is occasionally wrong
The hours it genuinely returns against every minute spent monitoring, fixing, and re-running it, since maintenance is often the largest lifetime cost
How many times it ran last month against how many times a teammate used it
questions.explanation: The lesson introduces total cost of ownership and warns that the savings are only the hours actually returned while the cost is every minute of monitoring, fixing, and re-running. When maintenance and re-checks edge out the savings, the workflow is a retirement candidate.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the single best way to get a tool to match the shape you want?
options: Show it one complete, filled-in example and tell it to match those exact field names
Explain in technical detail how JSON keys and values are parsed
Ask for a longer response so there is more material to work with
Leave the format unspecified so the tool uses its best judgment
questions.explanation: The lesson's fourth step for defining fields says the single best way to get a tool to match a shape is to show the finished shape once and ask for the same field names, so the downstream step reads cleanly with no relabeling. The other options contradict the lesson's emphasis on an explicit, consistent example.

questions.question: You are writing a decision record for choosing a monthly rather than weekly cadence. Which element does the lesson treat as the one that makes the record genuinely useful?
options: The condition under which you would reverse the decision, such as the input publishing weekly or a breach landing mid-month
A longer narrative explaining every option you considered and rejected in detail
An approval signature from a manager confirming the cadence was authorized
A screenshot of the scheduling configuration so the settings can be reproduced
questions.explanation: The lesson says the value sits in the third part of the record, what would change your mind, because a decision with no stated reversal condition can only be argued about rather than revisited honestly. Length and screenshots are not part of the format it gives.

questions.question: Priya re-runs her eleven-case golden set all at once and the tool starts refusing after six calls, even though she has plenty of use room left for the day. Per the lesson, what limit did she hit and how should she handle it?
options: A rate limit on requests per minute, and she should pace the calls by spreading them out across the morning or running fewer at a time
A context window limit, and she should reduce the size of the input
A hard spend limit, and she should raise her monthly cap
A quality-bar regression, and she should re-run the set after rolling back a prompt change
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that rate limits are measured across requests per minute and tokens per minute, and you can hit a request limit even when you have token allowance left. Priya fired the whole set at once and blew through requests per minute, not tokens. Because the re-run did not need one burst, she spaced the cases out and the limit stopped being a wall. A context window issue would drop content, a spend limit shows on the bill, and a regression changes output quality, not refuse calls.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is automation bias?
options: The tendency to favor the suggestions of an automated system over other information, even when the other information is correct
The tendency to distrust automation even when it is right, causing you to redo its work by hand
A technical error where the automation saves files to the wrong folder
The cost of maintaining a workflow that no longer earns its keep
questions.explanation: The lesson defines automation bias as favoring an automated system's suggestions over correct contradictory information, appearing as errors of omission (failing to act because the tool did not alert you) and errors of commission (following a wrong suggestion).

questions.question: The lesson warns that automation complacency can undo a well-placed review gate. What does this failure look like, and what does the lesson say is the defense?
options: The tool runs out of memory and silently drops a step, and the defense is to add more storage
The workflow skips the gate entirely on its own, and the defense is to re-run the workflow more often

Humans over-trust the system once it has been reliable, rationalize anomalies, and stop questioning outputs, and the defense is to design the gate so a genuine check is the path of least resistance rather than an act of willpower
The gate slows the workflow so much that no one wants to use it, and the defense is to remove the gate
questions.explanation: The lesson describes automation complacency as humans over-trusting a system, rationalizing anomalies, and stopping questioning its outputs; the more reliable the system appears, the less vigilant its overseers become. Because reliability itself breeds the skimming, the defense is structure: a gate built into the flow that hands the reviewer the information needed to decide and cannot be skipped, making a real check the path of least resistance. The stage is not about the tool failing storage, skipping steps on its own, or being too slow to use.

questions.question: Priya ran her monthly vendor summary in her tool's draft mode before sending it. Per the lesson, what made this a dry run?
options: It used her real input and produced the real output, but stopped before anything was sent, changed, or scheduled, so she saw the result with none of the consequences
It used made-up sample data so the real numbers were never touched at all
It sent the summary to a single test recipient and then to the full list
It skipped the review step entirely so the workflow ran faster
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a dry run as a run that uses your real input, produces the real output, and then stops before anything reaches the outside world, nothing is sent, changed, or scheduled. That is exactly what Priya's draft mode did. The other options describe either fake data, a partial real send, or skipping the check, none of which is a dry run.

questions.question: After running his post-mortem, Marcus wrote two action items: add a check that fails loudly on empty input, and add the data source's format to his runbook. Per the lesson, why are these action items the point of the whole exercise?
options: A post-mortem with no action items is a story, not a fix, because the follow-up actions with owners and deadlines are what prevent the failure from recurring
Action items are optional, since the real value of a post-mortem is the timeline that documents what happened
Action items only matter for team workflows, because a solo workflow owner does not need to track fixes
Action items should be written but never assigned, since assigning them creates blame
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that a post-mortem that ends with conclusions but no one assigned to act on them is a report, not a fix, and that the follow-up actions are the point. Google's SRE team treats the preventive actions as the measure of a post-mortem's worth. Action items with owners and deadlines are what turn a dead workflow into a lesson.

questions.question: A colleague asks you whether her output should be structured or free prose. Per the lesson, which single question settles it?
options: Who is doing the reading: a person who will act on it, or a spreadsheet, tracker, or automation
How many words the output should contain
Which chat tool generated the answer
Whether the answer contains any numbers at all
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by framing the whole art as one decision: decide who the consumer is. If a person will act on it, prose. If a spreadsheet, tracker, or any software will read it, structure. The other factors (length, tool, presence of numbers) are not the deciding question per the lesson.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is a handed-off connection between two software applications that lets them work together without a human relaying data?
options: An application programming interface (API), the agreed set of rules or protocols that lets two apps communicate and exchange data
A saved prompt that only works inside a single chat window
A spreadsheet template you copy figures into by hand each week
A manual export followed by a re-import into the next app
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an API as the agreed way two pieces of software talk to each other, the set of rules or protocols that enables apps to communicate and exchange data, per IBM. The other options describe the manual relay work a connected workflow removes.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the distinction between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop?
options: Human-in-the-loop stops the workflow until a person approves the output before it proceeds, while human-on-the-loop lets the workflow execute and a person monitors and steps in after the fact
There is no practical difference; the terms are interchangeable
Human-in-the-loop monitors output from the side, while human-on-the-loop is a required approval step inside the flow
Human-in-the-loop is for low-risk steps and human-on-the-loop is for high-risk steps
questions.explanation: The lesson defines human-in-the-loop as a model where the human must review, approve, or act on the output before any automated system proceeds, with the human decision inside the path and judgment a required step. Human-on-the-loop is the opposite: the workflow executes within policy limits and a human monitors from the side, stepping in to intervene after the fact. Confusing them matters because they fail differently, and the second kind fails quietly.

questions.question: Per the lesson, how does an ungoverned shared workflow become shadow AI?
options: It is shared using a free tool that the organization has not paid for
It produces output that differs slightly from the manual process for the same input
It runs on company data without a named owner, without a version, and without anyone checking what it is allowed to touch
It is used by more than three people at the same time
questions.explanation: The lesson defines shadow AI as AI workflows operating outside approved governance, security, or oversight. Sharing a workflow that runs on company data with no owner, no version, and no named data rules is the failure mode that turns sharing into shadow AI.

questions.question: Nadia's workflow has six steps: trigger, data pull, compute, draft, review gate, and output. Per the lesson, why does the review gate earn a pause while the data pull does not?
options: Because the report is externally visible and expensive to get wrong, so a human belongs in that loop, while the pull is routine and reversible and earns rhythm, not a pause
Because the data pull is the hardest step and needs a human to check every number
Because the review gate is the only step that produces any output at all
Because the trigger should always be the step that stops for human approval
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the review-gate test from Lesson 13: a step earns a pause when a miss costs too much. The report to leadership is externally visible and a wrong number in it is expensive to unwind, so it earns a gate. The data pull is routine and reversible, so it earns rhythm, not a pause. This is what keeps the workflow fast where it can be and careful where it must be. The other options reverse the reasoning.

questions.question: In the lesson, what is a queue for, and why does it matter?
options: It lets extra work line up and be processed in order at a steady pace when input arrives faster than the workflow can handle it, so nothing gets dropped during a rush
It makes the workflow run more often so spikes never build up
It processes every new item the moment it arrives instead of waiting
It replaces the schedule so the workflow only ever runs on events
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a message queue as a line where items are added on one end and taken off the other in arrival order, letting the sender hand off work and the receiver process it at its own pace. During a spike it absorbs the difference so the workflow clears the backlog without dropping any items. Running more often, immediate processing, or event-only triggers do not describe the queue's role.

questions.question: Nadia's weekly pricing scan came back with the over-five-percent flag column empty, even though she changed nothing in her prompt, input, or settings. Per the lesson, what is the most likely cause and the right first move?
options: Behavior drift: the model behind her tool was updated and stopped following part of her instruction, so she should run a known-good baseline input through the workflow and compare the output to catch the change
A deprecation: the vendor retired her model without notice, so she should immediately rewrite the whole workflow from scratch
A tool update she can see: the interface moved, so she should re-learn the new layout before doing anything else
A data error: her competitor URLs are stale, so she should replace them and re-run before suspecting the model
questions.explanation: The lesson describes exactly this as behavior drift: the same tool, prompt, and input produce different output because the model behind it changed, and the way to catch it is a smoke test that runs a known-good baseline input and compares the output. A deprecation is announced in advance, not silent, and the lesson says to check the baseline before rewriting or blaming the data.

questions.question: You are writing a runbook entry and you realize you are not sure what triggers one of your automations, only that it runs most mornings. Per the lesson, what should you write?
options: A polished sentence describing a trigger you assume, so the entry looks complete
Skip the trigger section entirely so the entry stays short
Write 'trigger unknown, need to check' and verify it, since a truthful entry with a gap is a roadmap while a silent guess is a trap
Remove the automation from your stack because you cannot explain it
questions.explanation: The lesson's try-it guidance says be honest: if you do not actually know what triggers the automation, write 'trigger unknown, need to check' and check it, because a truthful entry with a gap is a roadmap while a polished entry with a silent guess is a trap. Inventing a trigger, omitting it, or dropping the automation all contradict that.

questions.question: Priya asked her tool to write about a new vendor, and it produced a confident paragraph with a citation to a case study that turned out not to exist. Per the lesson, what is the right way to describe what happened?
options: A hallucination, a response that presents fabricated information as fact, such as a citation to a source that does not exist, and the fix is to verify the specific claim against something real
A silent error, because the tool reported success without sending an alert
A mid-flow break, because the tool stopped before finishing the paragraph
A versioning error, because the prompt had not been saved as a new version
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a hallucination as a response that presents fabricated information as fact, and notes that a large language model may embed plausible-sounding falsehoods such as fabricated citations. Priya's invented case study is the signature example. It is not a silent error (no stale data), not a mid-flow break (the tool finished), and not a versioning issue.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does a connected workflow need a review step at the end rather than shipping on its own?
options: Because an error in one link makes every later step wrong, and a confident-looking final output built on that mistake must be caught by a human before it matters
Because integrations cannot run without a person pressing a button to finish
Because the trigger will only fire when a human approves it first
Because downstream apps refuse to read output that was not human-reviewed
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that if step one is wrong, every step after it is wrong, so the output looks confident even when built on a mistake; the review stays at the end, keeping a human in the loop before the result matters, per the human-in-the-loop pattern.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what does the project knowledge base (saved context) do?
options: It is the space where uploaded reference material is used as context across chats in that project
It is a separate chat that runs without any instructions
It replaces the need for tailored instructions entirely
It automatically sends the output to your manager
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the project feature's support docs: anything added to the project knowledge base is used as context across the chats in that project, which is why the tool starts each run knowing your world instead of meeting it fresh.

questions.question: Dev's support-ticket prompt had drifted into a single wall of uncommented text. His manager reads the sections in a fixed order fix, and his weekly summary runs off the same prompt. Per the lesson, which habit is the one that makes the rest of the refactor possible?
options: Structure: dividing the prompt into labeled sections (role, audience, task, instructions, format, variable slot) with a consistent delimiter, so a reader can see which part does what
Making every instruction absolute so the model never has to interpret
Rewriting the whole prompt from scratch each week so it stays fresh
Removing the sections so the prompt reads as one continuous paragraph
questions.explanation: The lesson argues structure is the first habit because everything else depends on it: once the prompt is divided into labeled, delimited sections, you can tell the machine which text is a rule and which is data in, and you can read which part does what. Without structure there is no frame for maintainability or comments to live in.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the main benefit of a custom tool over retyping the same prompt each time?
options: It makes the tool start each conversation already knowing the instructions, the format, and the background, so you stop re-deciding those every time
It removes the need to review the output before it ships
It guarantees the tool never makes a mistake
It lets you skip defining the output of the workflow
questions.explanation: The lesson says a custom tool is the decision you make once and then stop making: it carries the standing instruction and context, so what you feed in shrinks to just the fresh facts. The review still stays with you and is not removed.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which task is the clearest fit for staying manual rather than running unattended?
options: A low-stakes, reversible, well-bounded routine that review would cost more than it saves
A high-stakes decision that is costly and hard to undo, so a human should sign off at the decision point
A task where the tools ability to draft a clean summary makes the output look reliable
Any task that has run cleanly for more than two months straight
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the test of how much a wrong result costs and how hard it is to undo. When both are high, the task stays manual or runs automated up to the decision point and stops for a person, which the cited Atlassian source ties to placing human checkpoints on actions hard to undo.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the key reason a step's output shape matters when you build a multi-step pipeline?
options: Each step's output becomes the next step's input, so a step that changes what it produces makes the downstream step read the wrong shape even if the change looks fine on its own
Steps only matter if the output is formatted as a polished document for a reader
A step's output shape only matters at the very end of the flow, never in the middle
Output shape is cosmetic and has no effect on whether the chain keeps working
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the handoff as the boundary where the output of one step becomes the input of the next, and warns that if any step changes what it produces, even in a way that looks fine alone, the downstream step reads the wrong shape and misbehaves in a way that looks like its fault. The other options contradict the core interface idea.

questions.question: Priya has four working workflows and wants her fifth to take a fraction of the time her first did. Per the lesson, what is the turning point that makes her fifth workflow cheap to build?
options: She memorizes the details of each workflow so she can rebuild them from memory faster
She extracts the general, proven pieces from her finished workflows into a reusable library she can assemble new workflows from
She works on one workflow each day so her speed improves through repetition
She copies the same prompt into every new workflow to make sure nothing is lost
questions.explanation: The lesson's whole point is that the fifth workflow is cheap because by then Priya reaches for saved templates, shared house-style instructions, structured-output contracts, and tested connectors from her library, so she does not solve those problems again. Memorizing, daily repetition, or copy-pasting the same prompt into everything describe duplication, the opposite of the compounding the lesson teaches.

questions.question: Priya's monthly vendor summary feeds a procurement review the team holds on the first Tuesday of each month. Per the lesson, how should she set its cadence?
options: Run it the morning of the review, so the output is ready when the decision that uses it is actually made
Run it every hour so the data is always as fresh as possible
Run it the day after the review so this month's work is already complete
Run it twice a day so nobody ever has to wait for an update
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that the right cadence is not the fastest one but the one that matches when the output gets used. Priya's review is the decision that uses the data, so she schedules the run for the morning of it. Hourly or extra runs produce the same result more often without improving it, and running after the review misses the decision it feeds.

questions.question: A workflow has a review step that says the owner 'reads the draft before it goes out.' Which change turns that habit into a gate, as the lesson defines it?
options: Name the specific checks, block the deliver step when any check fails, record the decision in the run log, and give the review a due time
Add a second person to read the draft as well
Add a reminder message that fires on the morning the digest is due
Move the review step earlier so there is more time to fix problems
questions.explanation: The lesson gives four tests for a gate: it names the check, it has a stop condition so delivery cannot proceed on failure, it records the decision, and it has an owner and a due time with a stale-review alarm. A reminder or a second reader leaves delivery unblocked.

questions.question: A minor patch to a tool Nadia uses fixes a bug she never hit, and her smoke test shows the workflow still produces the same output. Per the lesson, what should she do?
options: Ride the update out, because a change that her smoke test confirms does not affect her workflow needs no action
Adapt to it anyway, because every update should be treated as a reason to rewrite the workflow
Sunset the workflow, because any change to a tool is a sign the workflow is no longer worth keeping
Stop smoke-testing, because a patch that does not change output means the test is no longer needed
questions.explanation: The lesson says to ride it out when the change does not affect the workflow, and the discipline is to confirm that with a smoke test rather than assume it. Adapting to every update wastes time, sunsetting is only for workflows not worth keeping current, and the smoke test is exactly what lets her confirm the patch changed nothing.

questions.question: Per the lesson, when you design the pipeline from your scope, what is the right way to catch wiring mistakes before you connect anything?
options: Write down each step's input, action, and output in order, and fix any step whose output does not cleanly match the next step's input
Build all the steps first and run them together to see what breaks
Add error handling to every step before the first full run
Wire in the calendar trigger so real runs happen on schedule
questions.explanation: The lesson's design pass has you write the input, action, and output for each step in order. Because one step's output is the next step's input, writing them together is how you catch mismatches cheaply, before you wire anything.

questions.question: According to the lesson's Pareto framing, where should you point your workflow-building effort first?
options: At the largest or most interesting task, regardless of how often it happens
At the repetitive slice of your work, the roughly 20 percent of tasks with the same shape every time that carry most of the effort
At any task a colleague happens to mention, starting today
At the newest tool feature, to stay current
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the 80/20 rule to aim effort at the small slice of recurring, same-shape tasks, since that is where building a workflow pays for itself fastest.

questions.question: Priya's report ran all month with no errors and the model answered every request, but the monthly bill was four times her usual because she ran on a larger model and set no spend alert. Per the lesson, what is the cheapest protection she should have set in advance?
options: A spend alert at the amount she would want to know about, and a hard cap at the number she cannot afford to blow past, so the tool warns or stops her before the bill surprises her
A larger context window, so the report does not have to trim data
A higher requests-per-minute limit, so the golden set can run in one burst
A smaller golden set, so she re-runs fewer cases each time
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that a spend limit is the ceiling you choose yourself, and a spend alerts sends a notification while a hard limit makes requests fail when tracked spend reaches the configured amount, so the tool stops you instead of letting you find out in the mail. Priya had tracked quality and pacing but never cost, so nothing told her the bill was climbing. A larger context window and higher rate limit do not cap cost, and a smaller golden set does not address the larger-model cost.

questions.question: Priya's weekly client report runs once a day and a notification can wait. Per the lesson's reliability-to-task matching, what should she conclude about the reliability she actually needs?
options: She does not need a 99.999 percent service, and chasing one would cost her time and budget she does not have
She should require the most reliable tool available, since any downtime is unacceptable for a client report
She should abandon any tool below 99.9 percent availability, because that is the only acceptable standard
She should trust the newest tool regardless of its track record, because novelty implies better reliability
questions.explanation: The lesson, drawing on Google SRE's rule that a service should be made reliable enough but no more reliable than it needs to be, says Priya does not need extreme availability for a weekly report and that chasing it costs time and budget. The right move is to match the tool's reliability (and her fallback) to what the workflow actually needs.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does a content workflow need a content calendar as a single source of truth?
options: Because if Maya keeps her own copy of the week's plan, she would have two versions of the truth, and the workflow would eventually produce content for a cancelled piece or miss an added one, so she pulls from the one agreed place
Because a content calendar is only useful at the very end of the flow, never in the middle
Because keeping a separate list makes the workflow faster to produce each week
Because a content calendar only matters for social media posts, never for blog posts or emails
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the content calendar as the planning tool that tracks what you publish, when, and where, and treats it as the source of truth for the workflow. Maya pulls from the calendar rather than a list she maintains herself, because keeping her own copy would create two versions of the truth, and the workflow would eventually produce content for a piece that was cancelled or miss a piece that was added. The other options contradict the core idea.

questions.question: Priya found that one vendor row with a long, hyphenated name caused the tool to truncate the amount and make the total come up short. Per the lesson, what is this an example of?
options: An edge case, a problem that occurs only at an extreme operating parameter, like an input longer than the tool's comfortable range, rather than in its normal range
A happy path, the normal input where everything is in order
A versioning error, because the prompt had not been saved as a new version
A dry run failure, because the tool refused to produce any output
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an edge case as a problem that occurs only at an extreme operating parameter, the boundary of what a process can handle, and cites long, oddly formatted inputs as a classic example. Priya's long hyphenated vendor name is exactly that. The happy path is the normal input, so it is not this; the failure is not a versioning or dry-run issue.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why is the review the part that makes a workflow safe to rely on?
options: Because it keeps a human deciding at the point where the output could still be wrong, catching confident mistakes before they ship
Because it makes the workflow run faster by removing steps
Because it removes the need for a saved instruction
Because it lets the tool decide what to send without human input
questions.explanation: The lesson ties the review to human-in-the-loop: treat agent output as untrusted until your checks verify it. The review keeps a human deciding where the output could still be wrong, which is what makes the workflow safe.

questions.question: In Maya's content workflow, why does the review gate sit before the repurpose step rather than after it?
options: Because if the tool repurposed an unchecked draft, a wrong claim in the blog post would silently propagate into every social post and the email, multiplying the error instead of catching it
Because the repurpose step is the only step that produces any output at all
Because the data pull is the hardest step and needs a human to check every piece
Because the trigger should always be the step that stops for human approval
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that Maya decided the tool could repurpose her blog post into social posts and the email, but only after the blog post itself was approved. If the tool repurposed a draft that had not been checked, a wrong claim in the blog post would silently propagate into every social post and the email, multiplying the error instead of catching it. The gate sits before the repurpose step for exactly that reason. The other options reverse the reasoning.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what does a comment on a prompt rule record that the rule itself usually does not?
options: The why: the reason the rule exists, the incident or constraint that decided it, so a future reader knows whether the reason still holds before they touch the rule
A longer, more detailed restatement of the same instruction
A second copy of the rule in different words so the model sees it twice
Nothing; comments are only for the model, never for a human reader
questions.explanation: The lesson says a comment records why a rule exists, not just what it does, the reason that a future reader or a future you needs to know before editing. Restating the rule adds nothing, duplicating it couples the rules together, and the comments' second audience is a human reader, with the why-line also helping the model weigh the rule by intent.
